title: Cut the Number of Choices You Make Each Day
title_full: Cut the number of choices you make each day. Your brain will thank you
subtitle: Decision Fatigue, Satisficing & Focus — Reading Courseware
source: By Associated Press, adapted by Newsela staff on 08.24.26
article_lead: Hundreds of studies show that too many options stress people, leave them stuck, and make them less happy with what they pick. Psychologists Barry Schwartz and Daniel Willingham argue that the brain prefers memory to hard thinking — and that satisficing, Herbert Simon's rule of "good enough, then move on," can boost focus, satisfaction, and free time.
article_full:
Opening
The perfect shirt. The movie to watch tonight. Your best friend. There are all kinds of choices that people make every day. Scientists have done hundreds of studies on choices. This research shows having too many options is not a good thing. More choices can stress people and leave them unable to decide. It can also make people less happy with their choices, said Barry Schwartz. He used to teach psychology. To make things easier for your mind, he said, limit the number of choices you make. Your brain will thank you.

More Is Often More Confusing
Schwartz gave a few examples of studies about decision-making. Many companies offer plans to help workers save money for the future. One popular plan is a 401(k). But researchers found that when a company offers many plans, fewer workers sign up. Less important choices showed similar patterns. One study looked at how grocery choices affected shoppers. It found people bought more jars of jam when they had six choices instead of 24. In another study, students were more likely to finish an extra-credit assignment when they had six topics. Fewer students wanted the extra credit when they had to choose from 30 topics.

Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions
Schwartz said that too many choices can make people feel stuck. People might also make poorer decisions. That's because more options increase the chances of bad outcomes. Even if they make a good choice, they might worry there was a better one. Not all people are like this all the time, Schwartz added. Car enthusiasts love car details. They will happily review the information for every car when buying a new one. "But you don't feel that way when it comes to buying jam," he said.

The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions
Daniel Willingham is also a psychology professor. He said the brain actually tries to stop us from thinking too much. Solving problems uses more energy than remembering things. This idea comes from how humans survived long ago. When we have a goal, the brain first remembers what worked before. This came from our ancestors reacting to danger or finding a place to stay. It only starts solving problems if it has to. "Another way to put it is that if you're thinking, things are not going well," Willingham said. This is why people often do things without thinking much. They could try something new, like taking a different way to work. But they usually don't. Schwartz said the problem of having too many choices is also part of our daily lives. Social media makes it worse. Online, everyone can easily compare their choices to others. If you have two options for jeans, "nobody expects the jeans they buy to fit perfectly," Schwartz said. "When there are 2,000 options… Now, you do expect your jeans to fit perfectly."

Limit Your Choices And Move On
David Epstein used to be a maximalist. Now he limits his opportunities to make choices. Once, he bought 10 of the same well-fitting T-shirts in different colors. He followed Herbert Simon's example. Simon was a famous thinker. He only had three sets of clothes and ate almost the same thing every day. Simon created the word "satisficing," which means picking something that is good enough and then moving on. Epstein sets satisficing rules for himself when shopping online. He thinks about why he is buying something and doesn't read reviews. Willingham and Schwartz suggest looking to people in your life to help, too. If you need a new phone, ask a friend who likes theirs. Changing how you make choices is hard, but it helps. "Over time … you find it easier to make decisions," Schwartz said. "You end up more satisfied with the decisions you make." And, he added, you get more free time.

grade10.sentence: The article links fewer decisions not only to speed, but to peace of mind.
grade10.translation: 文章把更少的决策不仅与速度联系起来，也与内心平静联系起来。

phrases.definition_en: To put money aside so you can use it later.

article_example.sentence: Many companies offer plans to help workers save money for the future.
article_example.translation: 许多公司提供计划，帮助员工为将来存钱。

zhongkao.sentence: She tries to save money for the future every month.
zhongkao.translation: 她每月努力为将来存钱。

grade10.sentence: Ironically, offering more ways to save money for the future made fewer workers start at all.
grade10.translation: 吊诡的是，为将来存钱的途径越多，开始存钱的员工反而更少。

phrases.definition_en: People who love cars and enjoy studying their details.

article_example.sentence: Car enthusiasts love car details.
article_example.translation: 汽车爱好者喜欢汽车的各种细节。

zhongkao.sentence: Car enthusiasts spent the afternoon comparing engines.
zhongkao.translation: 汽车爱好者一下午都在比较发动机。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz uses car enthusiasts as the exception: they enjoy details most people find tiring.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨把汽车爱好者当作例外：他们享受多数人觉得累人的细节。

phrases.definition_en: In an automatic way; not pausing to solve a new problem.
phrases.definition_cn: 不怎么思考地；不假思索地

article_example.sentence: This is why people often do things without thinking much.
article_example.translation: 这就是为什么人们常常不怎么思考就做事。

zhongkao.sentence: He took the same road without thinking much.
zhongkao.translation: 他不怎么思考就走了同一条路。

grade10.sentence: Willingham’s point is evolutionary: doing things without thinking much once kept ancestors safe.
grade10.translation: 威林厄姆的观点带有演化色彩：不怎么思考地行事，曾让祖先更安全。

phrases.definition_en: Time when you are not working or studying.

article_example.sentence: And, he added, you get more free time.
article_example.translation: 他还补充说，你会得到更多空闲时间。

zhongkao.sentence: I use my free time to read history.
zhongkao.translation: 我用空闲时间读历史。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz’s last gain is practical: better decisions and more free time.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨指出的最后一层收益很实际：更好的决定，以及更多空闲时间。

article_example.sentence: Over time you find it easier to make decisions.
article_example.translation: 随着时间推移，你会发现做决定变得更容易。

zhongkao.sentence: Over time, her English became more natural.
zhongkao.translation: 随着时间推移，她的英语变得更自然。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz does not promise a sudden change; over time the habit of limiting choices gets easier.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨并不承诺突然改变；随着时间推移，限制选择的习惯会变得更容易。

phrases.other_usage: over time you find it easier

phrases.definition_en: A U.S. workplace plan that helps employees save money for later life.

article_example.sentence: One popular plan is a 401(k).
article_example.translation: 一种常见的计划是 401(k)。

zhongkao.sentence: Her first job offered a 401(k) for retirement savings.
zhongkao.translation: 她的第一份工作提供了 401(k) 退休储蓄。

grade10.sentence: When firms offered many 401(k) plans, fewer workers signed up — a costly kind of confusion.
grade10.translation: 公司提供的 401(k) 计划太多时，报名的员工更少——这是一种代价很高的困惑。

phrases.definition_en: Additional points a teacher offers beyond required work.

article_example.sentence: Fewer students wanted the extra credit when they had to choose from 30 topics.
article_example.translation: 当必须从 30 个题目中选择时，想要额外学分的学生更少。

zhongkao.sentence: He asked the teacher if extra credit was still available.
zhongkao.translation: 他问老师是否还有额外学分。

grade10.sentence: The extra-credit study mirrors the jam study: six topics beat thirty.
grade10.translation: 额外学分研究和果酱研究镜像：六个题目胜过三十个。

phrases.definition_en: The right size and shape for the body.

article_example.sentence: Once, he bought 10 of the same well-fitting T-shirts in different colors.
article_example.translation: 有一次，他买了十件同样合身、颜色不同的 T 恤。

zhongkao.sentence: She finally found a well-fitting pair of shoes.
zhongkao.translation: 她终于找到一双合身的鞋。

grade10.sentence: Epstein’s well-fitting T-shirts are a satisficing tool: decide once, repeat the win.
grade10.translation: 爱泼斯坦那些合身的 T 恤是 satisficing 工具：决定一次，重复这个胜利。

patterns.word: Having too many X is not a good thing
patterns.definition_en: States that an excess of something causes harm.
patterns.definition_cn: 拥有过多的……并不是好事

article_example.sentence: This research shows having too many options is not a good thing.
article_example.translation: 这项研究表明，选项过多并不是好事。

zhongkao.sentence: Having too many after-school clubs is not a good thing if you cannot rest.
zhongkao.translation: 如果无法休息，课后社团过多并不是好事。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz’s line is generalizable: having too many options is not a good thing for most minds.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨的判断可以推广：对大多数人的大脑而言，选项过多并不是好事。

patterns.other_usage: Having too many X is not a good thing

patterns.word: More X can Y and leave them unable to Z
patterns.definition_en: Shows that an increase causes stress and blocks action.
patterns.definition_cn: 更多的……会……并使他们无法……

article_example.sentence: More choices can stress people and leave them unable to decide.
article_example.translation: 更多选择会给人带来压力，并让他们无法做决定。

zhongkao.sentence: More homework can tire students and leave them unable to sleep.
zhongkao.translation: 更多作业会使学生疲惫，并让他们无法入睡。

grade10.sentence: The structure pairs a feeling (stress) with a failure to act (unable to decide).
grade10.translation: 这个结构把感受（压力）和行动失败（无法决定）绑在一起。

patterns.other_usage: More X can Y and leave them unable to Z

patterns.word: When a company offers many X, fewer Y
patterns.definition_en: A cause-and-effect pattern: more supply, less uptake.

article_example.sentence: When a company offers many plans, fewer workers sign up.
article_example.translation: 当公司提供许多计划时，报名的员工反而更少。

zhongkao.sentence: When a library offers many reading lists, fewer students finish one.
zhongkao.translation: 当图书馆提供许多书单时，读完一本的学生反而更少。

grade10.sentence: The 401(k) finding is the same paradox: more plans, fewer workers sign up.
grade10.translation: 401(k) 的发现是同一悖论：计划越多，报名的员工越少。

patterns.other_usage: When A offers many X, fewer Y

patterns.word: The brain first... It only ... if it has to
patterns.definition_en: Describes a default mental shortcut, then a last resort.
patterns.definition_cn: 大脑先……；只有在不得已时才……

article_example.sentence: When we have a goal, the brain first remembers what worked before. It only starts solving problems if it has to.
article_example.translation: 当我们有一个目标时，大脑会先回忆以前什么方法有效。它只有在不得已时才开始解决问题。

zhongkao.sentence: When I lose my key, I first check my bag. I only search the whole house if I have to.
zhongkao.translation: 钥匙丢了，我先检查书包。只有不得已时才翻遍整栋房子。

grade10.sentence: Willingham’s model is economical: memory first; new thinking only if it has to.
grade10.translation: 威林厄姆的模型很节省：先记忆；只有不得已才进行新思考。

patterns.other_usage: The brain first... It only ... if it has to

patterns.word: When there are 2,000 options, now you expect...
patterns.definition_en: Shows how a huge menu raises standards to an impossible level.
patterns.definition_cn: 当有两千种选项时，你就会指望……

article_example.sentence: When there are 2,000 options… Now, you do expect your jeans to fit perfectly.
article_example.translation: 当有两千种选项时……现在，你就会指望牛仔裤完美合身。

zhongkao.sentence: When there are 2,000 online courses, now you expect one to match you perfectly.
zhongkao.translation: 当有两千门在线课程时，你就会指望其中一门完美适合你。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz’s jeans line is the social-media punch: more options inflate expectation.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨关于牛仔裤的句子是社交媒体的一击：选项越多，期望越高。

patterns.other_usage: When there are N options, now you expect...

patterns.word: picking something that is good enough and then moving on
patterns.definition_en: Defines satisficing as a two-step rule.
patterns.definition_cn: 选一个够好的，然后继续往前走

article_example.sentence: Satisficing means picking something that is good enough and then moving on.
article_example.translation: satisficing 的意思是选一个够好的，然后继续往前走。

zhongkao.sentence: For lunch I am picking something that is good enough and then moving on.
zhongkao.translation: 午餐我选一个够好的，然后继续往前走。

grade10.sentence: Simon’s definition has two verbs on purpose: pick, then move — not pick, then keep searching.
grade10.translation: 西蒙的定义故意用了两个动作：先选，再走——而不是选完还继续找。

patterns.other_usage: pick something good enough and then move on

all_vocab_items.definition_en: The act of picking one thing from two or more possibilities; the thing you pick.

article_example.sentence: There are all kinds of choices that people make every day.
article_example.translation: 人们每天都会做出各种各样的选择。

zhongkao.sentence: You have a choice between tea and coffee.
zhongkao.translation: 你可以在茶和咖啡之间做选择。

grade10.sentence: Too many choices can leave people less happy with what they finally pick.
grade10.translation: 选择过多可能让人对最终所选更不满意。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: make a choice 做出选择

all_vocab_items.definition_en: One possible thing you can choose.

article_example.sentence: This research shows having too many options is not a good thing.
article_example.translation: 这项研究表明，选项过多并不是好事。

zhongkao.sentence: The menu gives three options for lunch.
zhongkao.translation: 菜单上有三种午餐选项。

grade10.sentence: More options increase the chances of bad outcomes, Schwartz said.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨说，选项越多，出现糟糕结果的可能性也越大。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: too many options 选项过多

all_vocab_items.definition_en: A choice you make after thinking about what to do.

article_example.sentence: Over time you find it easier to make decisions.
article_example.translation: 随着时间推移，你会发现做决定变得更容易。

zhongkao.sentence: She made a decision to join the school choir.
zhongkao.translation: 她决定加入学校合唱团。

grade10.sentence: Reducing daily decisions can leave people more satisfied with the ones they keep.
grade10.translation: 减少日常决策可以让人对留下的那些决定更满意。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: Careful study to find out new facts or test ideas.

article_example.sentence: This research shows having too many options is not a good thing.
article_example.translation: 这项研究表明，选项过多并不是好事。

zhongkao.sentence: Their research on sleep helped change school start times.
zhongkao.translation: 他们对睡眠的研究推动了学校上课时间的调整。

grade10.sentence: Hundreds of studies form the research behind Schwartz's advice to limit choices.
grade10.translation: 数百项研究构成了施瓦茨“限制选择”建议背后的研究基础。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: To put pressure on someone; the worried feeling that pressure causes.

article_example.sentence: More choices can stress people and leave them unable to decide.
article_example.translation: 更多选择会给人带来压力，并让他们无法做决定。

zhongkao.sentence: Too much homework can stress students before exams.
zhongkao.translation: 作业过多会在考试前给学生带来压力。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz argues that a flood of options can stress the mind and reduce happiness.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨认为，海量选项会给大脑施压并降低幸福感。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: stress people 给人带来压力

all_vocab_items.definition_en: The scientific study of the mind and how people think, feel, and act.

article_example.sentence: He used to teach psychology.
article_example.translation: 他曾教授心理学。

zhongkao.sentence: She wants to study psychology at university.
zhongkao.translation: 她想在大学学习心理学。

grade10.sentence: Both Schwartz and Willingham draw on psychology to explain why extra options tire the brain.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨和威林厄姆都借助心理学来解释为何额外选项会让大脑疲惫。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: To keep the number or amount of something from becoming too large.

article_example.sentence: To make things easier for your mind, he said, limit the number of choices you make.
article_example.translation: 他说，为了让大脑更轻松，要限制自己做选择的数量。

zhongkao.sentence: Teachers limit phone use during class.
zhongkao.translation: 老师限制课堂上使用手机。

grade10.sentence: Epstein now limits his opportunities to make choices so shopping takes less energy.
grade10.translation: 爱泼斯坦现在限制自己做选择的机会，好让购物少耗精力。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: limit the number of 限制……的数量

all_vocab_items.definition_en: Difficult to understand because there is too much information or too many choices.

article_example.sentence: More Is Often More Confusing
article_example.translation: 更多往往更令人困惑

zhongkao.sentence: The new map was confusing at first.
zhongkao.translation: 这张新地图起初令人困惑。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz's studies suggest that a longer list of plans is more confusing, so fewer workers sign up.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨的研究表明，计划清单越长越令人困惑，因此报名的员工更少。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: A regular way in which something happens again and again.

article_example.sentence: Less important choices showed similar patterns.
article_example.translation: 不那么重要的选择也呈现出类似的模式。

zhongkao.sentence: We noticed a pattern: students who sleep more score higher.
zhongkao.translation: 我们注意到一个规律：睡眠更多的学生分数更高。

grade10.sentence: Jam, extra credit, and 401(k) plans all follow the same pattern: more options, fewer actions.
grade10.translation: 果酱、额外学分和 401(k) 计划都遵循同一模式：选项越多，行动越少。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: The result of a choice, action, or situation.

article_example.sentence: That's because more options increase the chances of bad outcomes.
article_example.translation: 那是因为选项越多，出现糟糕结果的可能性也越大。

zhongkao.sentence: The outcome of the experiment surprised the class.
zhongkao.translation: 实验结果让全班感到意外。

grade10.sentence: More options raise the chance of a bad outcome and of later regret.
grade10.translation: 选项越多，糟糕结果和事后后悔的可能性就越大。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: A person who is very interested in a subject and enjoys its details.

article_example.sentence: Car enthusiasts love car details.
article_example.translation: 汽车爱好者喜欢汽车的各种细节。

zhongkao.sentence: A music enthusiast collected records from many countries.
zhongkao.translation: 一位音乐爱好者收集了来自许多国家的唱片。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz notes that car enthusiasts will review every model, but most people do not feel that way about jam.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨指出，汽车爱好者会研究每一款车，但多数人对果酱不会有这种热情。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: The strength the body or mind uses to do work.

article_example.sentence: Solving problems uses more energy than remembering things.
article_example.translation: 解决问题比回忆事物更耗费精力。

zhongkao.sentence: A good breakfast gives you energy for morning classes.
zhongkao.translation: 一顿好早餐能给你上午上课的精力。

grade10.sentence: Willingham says problem-solving costs more mental energy, so the brain prefers memory first.
grade10.translation: 威林厄姆说，解决问题更耗心智精力，所以大脑会优先调用记忆。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: use more energy 耗费更多精力

all_vocab_items.definition_en: A person in your family who lived long ago; early humans in this article.

article_example.sentence: This came from our ancestors reacting to danger or finding a place to stay.
article_example.translation: 这来自我们的祖先对危险做出反应或寻找落脚之处。

zhongkao.sentence: My ancestors moved to this city a hundred years ago.
zhongkao.translation: 我的祖先一百年前迁到了这座城市。

grade10.sentence: The brain's shortcut — remember first, think later — helped ancestors survive danger.
grade10.translation: 大脑“先回忆、后思考”的捷径曾帮助祖先在危险中生存。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: To look at two or more things to see how they are similar or different.

article_example.sentence: Online, everyone can easily compare their choices to others.
article_example.translation: 在网上，每个人都能轻易把自己的选择和别人比较。

zhongkao.sentence: Please compare the two poems and find their differences.
zhongkao.translation: 请比较这两首诗并找出不同。

grade10.sentence: Social media lets people compare jeans, phones, and holidays until nothing feels good enough.
grade10.translation: 社交媒体让人们比较牛仔裤、手机和假期，直到没有什么再显得足够好。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: compare A to B 把 A 与 B 比较

all_vocab_items.definition_en: To believe that something should happen or should be a certain way.

article_example.sentence: Nobody expects the jeans they buy to fit perfectly.
article_example.translation: 没有人指望买到的牛仔裤能完美合身。

zhongkao.sentence: We expect the train to arrive at six.
zhongkao.translation: 我们预计火车六点到达。

grade10.sentence: When there are 2,000 options, people expect the jeans they buy to fit perfectly.
grade10.translation: 当有两千种选项时，人们就会指望买到的牛仔裤完美合身。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: expect sth. to do 期望某物……

all_vocab_items.definition_en: A chance to do something.

article_example.sentence: Now he limits his opportunities to make choices.
article_example.translation: 现在他限制自己做选择的机会。

zhongkao.sentence: The contest is a good opportunity to practice English.
zhongkao.translation: 这次比赛是练习英语的好机会。

grade10.sentence: Epstein cuts opportunities to choose so that small purchases do not eat the day.
grade10.translation: 爱泼斯坦减少做选择的机会，以免小购物耗掉一整天。

all_vocab_items.definition_en: To look at information carefully again before deciding.

article_example.sentence: They will happily review the information for every car when buying a new one.
article_example.translation: 买新车时，他们会乐意审阅每一款车的信息。

zhongkao.sentence: Please review your notes before the test.
zhongkao.translation: 考试前请复习笔记。

grade10.sentence: Car enthusiasts review every detail; Epstein refuses to review endless online comments.
grade10.translation: 汽车爱好者会审阅每个细节；爱泼斯坦则拒绝翻看无穷无尽的网上评论。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: review the information 审阅信息

all_vocab_items.definition_en: Pleased because something is good enough.

article_example.sentence: You end up more satisfied with the decisions you make.
article_example.translation: 你最终会对自己做的决定更满意。

zhongkao.sentence: She was satisfied with her science project.
zhongkao.translation: 她对自己的科学作业感到满意。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz claims that people who limit choices end up more satisfied, not less ambitious.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨认为，限制选择的人最终会更满意，而不是更没追求。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: more satisfied with 对……更满意

all_vocab_items.definition_en: To increase or improve something.

article_example.sentence: Reducing the number of decisions you make each day can boost your focus and peace of mind.
article_example.translation: 减少每天做决定的数量可以提升你的专注力和内心平静。

zhongkao.sentence: Morning exercise can boost your energy at school.
zhongkao.translation: 晨练可以提升你在学校的精力。

grade10.sentence: The article argues that fewer daily decisions boost focus rather than making life poorer.
grade10.translation: 文章认为，减少日常决策能提升专注，而不是让生活变差。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: boost your focus 提升专注力

all_vocab_items.definition_en: The ability to give all your attention to one thing.

article_example.sentence: Reducing the number of decisions you make each day can boost your focus and peace of mind.
article_example.translation: 减少每天做决定的数量可以提升你的专注力和内心平静。

zhongkao.sentence: Please keep your focus on the teacher's question.
zhongkao.translation: 请把注意力集中在老师的问题上。

grade10.sentence: Schwartz's point is practical: fewer trivial choices free focus for work that matters.
grade10.translation: 施瓦茨的观点很实际：减少琐碎选择，就能把专注留给真正重要的事。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: boost your focus 提升专注力

all_vocab_items.definition_en: To make something smaller in number or amount.

article_example.sentence: Reducing the number of decisions you make each day can boost your focus and peace of mind.
article_example.translation: 减少每天做决定的数量可以提升你的专注力和内心平静。

zhongkao.sentence: We should reduce plastic waste at school.
zhongkao.translation: 我们应减少学校里的塑料垃圾。

grade10.sentence: The title's advice is to reduce daily decisions so the brain has less to manage.
grade10.translation: 标题的建议是减少日常决策，让大脑少负担一些。

all_vocab_items.other_usage: reduce the number of 减少……的数量

all_vocab_items.definition_en: A person who wants as many options or as much as possible.
all_vocab_items.definition_cn: 最大化主义者；什么都想要的人

article_example.sentence: David Epstein used to be a maximalist.
article_example.translation: 戴维·爱泼斯坦曾经是一个最大化主义者。

zhongkao.sentence: A maximalist fills a closet with clothes but still feels nothing is right.
zhongkao.translation: 最大化主义者把衣橱塞满衣服，却仍觉得没有一件合适。

grade10.sentence: Epstein stopped being a maximalist and began using satisficing rules when he shopped.
grade10.translation: 爱泼斯坦不再做最大化主义者，购物时开始使用“够好就行”的规则。

paragraphs.title: Opening
sentences: The perfect shirt. The movie to watch tonight. Your best friend. There are all kinds of choices that people make every day.
Scientists have done hundreds of studies on choices.
This research shows having too many options is not a good thing.
More choices can stress people and leave them unable to decide.
It can also make people less happy with their choices, said Barry Schwartz.
He used to teach psychology.
To make things easier for your mind, he said, limit the number of choices you make.
Your brain will thank you.

socratic.q: What everyday examples of choices does the opening give?
socratic.a: The perfect shirt, the movie to watch tonight, and your best friend — kinds of choices people make every day.

socratic.q: According to the research Schwartz cites, what do too many options do to people?
socratic.a: They can stress people, leave them unable to decide, and make them less happy with their choices.

socratic.q: What is Schwartz's first piece of advice?
socratic.a: Limit the number of choices you make so your mind has an easier time — "your brain will thank you."

paragraphs.title: Studies of Too Many Options
sentences: Schwartz gave a few examples of studies about decision-making.
Many companies offer plans to help workers save money for the future.
One popular plan is a 401(k).
But researchers found that when a company offers many plans, fewer workers sign up.
Less important choices showed similar patterns.
One study looked at how grocery choices affected shoppers.
It found people bought more jars of jam when they had six choices instead of 24.
In another study, students were more likely to finish an extra-credit assignment when they had six topics.
Fewer students wanted the extra credit when they had to choose from 30 topics.

socratic.q: What happened when companies offered many 401(k) plans?
socratic.a: Fewer workers signed up, even though the plans were meant to help them save money for the future.

socratic.q: What did the jam study find?
socratic.a: Shoppers bought more jars of jam when they had six choices instead of 24.

socratic.q: How did the extra-credit study match the jam study?
socratic.a: Students were more likely to finish the assignment with six topics; fewer wanted extra credit when they had 30 topics.

paragraphs.title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions
sentences: Schwartz said that too many choices can make people feel stuck.
People might also make poorer decisions.
That's because more options increase the chances of bad outcomes.
Even if they make a good choice, they might worry there was a better one.
Not all people are like this all the time, Schwartz added.
Car enthusiasts love car details.
They will happily review the information for every car when buying a new one.
"But you don't feel that way when it comes to buying jam," he said.

socratic.q: Besides feeling stuck, what second harm can too many options cause?
socratic.a: People might make poorer decisions because more options increase the chances of bad outcomes.

socratic.q: Why might someone still feel unhappy after a good choice?
socratic.a: They might worry there was a better option they did not take.

socratic.q: Who is the exception Schwartz mentions, and what is his contrast?
socratic.a: Car enthusiasts enjoy reviewing every car; most people do not feel that way when buying jam.

paragraphs.title: The Brain and Social Media
paragraphs.section_heading: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions
sentences: Daniel Willingham is also a psychology professor.
He said the brain actually tries to stop us from thinking too much.
Solving problems uses more energy than remembering things.
This idea comes from how humans survived long ago.
When we have a goal, the brain first remembers what worked before.
This came from our ancestors reacting to danger or finding a place to stay.
It only starts solving problems if it has to.
"Another way to put it is that if you're thinking, things are not going well," Willingham said.
This is why people often do things without thinking much.
They could try something new, like taking a different way to work.
But they usually don't.
Schwartz said the problem of having too many choices is also part of our daily lives.
Social media makes it worse.
Online, everyone can easily compare their choices to others.
If you have two options for jeans, "nobody expects the jeans they buy to fit perfectly," Schwartz said.
"When there are 2,000 options… Now, you do expect your jeans to fit perfectly."

socratic.q: According to Willingham, why do people repeat familiar actions instead of trying something new?
socratic.a: Solving problems uses more energy than remembering things, so the brain first uses what worked before and only thinks hard if it has to.

socratic.q: What does Willingham mean by "if you're thinking, things are not going well"?
socratic.a: Hard thinking is a backup system; the brain treats new problem-solving as a sign that the usual path is not working.

socratic.q: How does social media raise people's expectations?
socratic.a: Online comparison makes 2,000 options feel normal, so people expect jeans (and other goods) to fit perfectly.

paragraphs.title: Satisficing and Moving On
paragraphs.section_heading: Limit Your Choices And Move On
sentences: David Epstein used to be a maximalist.
Now he limits his opportunities to make choices.
Once, he bought 10 of the same well-fitting T-shirts in different colors.
He followed Herbert Simon's example.
Simon was a famous thinker.
He only had three sets of clothes and ate almost the same thing every day.
Simon created the word "satisficing," which means picking something that is good enough and then moving on.
Epstein sets satisficing rules for himself when shopping online.
He thinks about why he is buying something and doesn't read reviews.
Willingham and Schwartz suggest looking to people in your life to help, too.
If you need a new phone, ask a friend who likes theirs.
Changing how you make choices is hard, but it helps.
"Over time … you find it easier to make decisions," Schwartz said.
"You end up more satisfied with the decisions you make."
And, he added, you get more free time.

socratic.q: What is satisficing, and who created the word?
socratic.a: Herbert Simon created it; it means picking something that is good enough and then moving on.

socratic.q: How do Epstein and Simon put satisficing into daily life?
socratic.a: Simon had three sets of clothes and ate almost the same food; Epstein bought 10 well-fitting T-shirts and does not read online reviews.

socratic.q: What three gains does Schwartz promise if people change how they choose?
socratic.a: Decisions get easier over time, people feel more satisfied, and they get more free time.

all_sentences.paragraph_title: More Is Often More Confusing

all_sentences.text: It found people bought more jars of jam when they had six choices instead of 24.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: More Is Often More Confusing

all_sentences.text: In another study, students were more likely to finish an extra-credit assignment when they had six topics.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: More Is Often More Confusing

all_sentences.text: Fewer students wanted the extra credit when they had to choose from 30 topics.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: More Is Often More Confusing

all_sentences.text: Schwartz said that too many choices can make people feel stuck.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: People might also make poorer decisions.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: That's because more options increase the chances of bad outcomes.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: Even if they make a good choice, they might worry there was a better one.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: Not all people are like this all the time, Schwartz added.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: Car enthusiasts love car details.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: They will happily review the information for every car when buying a new one.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: "But you don't feel that way when it comes to buying jam," he said.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Stuck, Regret, and Exceptions

all_sentences.text: Daniel Willingham is also a psychology professor.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: He said the brain actually tries to stop us from thinking too much.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: Solving problems uses more energy than remembering things.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: This idea comes from how humans survived long ago.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: When we have a goal, the brain first remembers what worked before.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: This came from our ancestors reacting to danger or finding a place to stay.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: It only starts solving problems if it has to.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: "Another way to put it is that if you're thinking, things are not going well," Willingham said.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: This is why people often do things without thinking much.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: They could try something new, like taking a different way to work.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: But they usually don't.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: Schwartz said the problem of having too many choices is also part of our daily lives.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: Social media makes it worse.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: Online, everyone can easily compare their choices to others.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: If you have two options for jeans, "nobody expects the jeans they buy to fit perfectly," Schwartz said.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: "When there are 2,000 options… Now, you do expect your jeans to fit perfectly."
all_sentences.paragraph_title: The Brain Doesn't Like Making Decisions

all_sentences.text: David Epstein used to be a maximalist.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: Now he limits his opportunities to make choices.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: Once, he bought 10 of the same well-fitting T-shirts in different colors.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: He followed Herbert Simon's example.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: Simon was a famous thinker.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: He only had three sets of clothes and ate almost the same thing every day.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: Simon created the word "satisficing," which means picking something that is good enough and then moving on.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: Epstein sets satisficing rules for himself when shopping online.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: He thinks about why he is buying something and doesn't read reviews.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: Willingham and Schwartz suggest looking to people in your life to help, too.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: If you need a new phone, ask a friend who likes theirs.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: Changing how you make choices is hard, but it helps.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: "Over time … you find it easier to make decisions," Schwartz said.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: "You end up more satisfied with the decisions you make."
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

all_sentences.text: And, he added, you get more free time.
all_sentences.paragraph_title: Limit Your Choices And Move On

graphic_organizer.title: Cut the Number of Choices — Text Structure

sections.heading: Main Idea
sections.content: Too many options stress people and make them less happy; limiting choices and satisficing (good enough, then move on) ease decisions and free time.

sections.heading: Section 1: Opening
sections.content: Everyday choices pile up; Schwartz's research says excess options stress people, freeze decisions, and reduce happiness — so limit them.

sections.heading: Section 2: More Is Often More Confusing
sections.content: 401(k) plans, jam (6 vs 24), and extra credit (6 vs 30) show the same pattern: more options, less action.

sections.heading: Section 3: Stuck and Exceptions
sections.content: Too many choices leave people stuck, raise bad outcomes, and invite regret; car enthusiasts are the exception, jam buyers are not.

sections.heading: Section 4: The Brain and Social Media
sections.content: Willingham: the brain saves energy by remembering first; social media comparison makes 2,000 options feel like jeans must fit perfectly.

sections.heading: Section 5: Limit and Move On
sections.content: Epstein and Simon practice satisficing; ask a friend; over time decisions get easier, satisfaction rises, and free time returns.
